lessons.title: What is a Decimal?
lessons.intro: A decimal is a way to write numbers that are between whole numbers — like the money in your pocket, which is rupees AND paise!
explanation: A decimal point separates the whole part from the fraction part.
In 3.5, the 3 is whole and the .5 means half.
Decimals are just another way to write fractions with 10, 100, 1000.
lessons.rule: The decimal point separates whole numbers from parts.
lessons.tip: Read 3.5 as 'three point five'.

steps.text: A decimal splits whole and part at the point.
Tenths are the first place after the point.

lessons.title: Tenths
lessons.intro: The very first place after the decimal point is the tenths place — one whole split into 10 equal parts.
explanation: 0.1 means one tenth, written 1/10.
0.7 means seven tenths, or 7/10.
Ten tenths make one whole: 0.1 x 10 = 1.
lessons.rule: The first decimal place is tenths (1/10).
lessons.tip: 0.1 is one slice of a ten-slice cake.

lessons.title: Decimals and Money
lessons.intro: Rupees and paise are decimals in real life — 100 paise make 1 rupee.
explanation: Rs 3.50 means 3 rupees and 50 paise.
The two digits after the point are the paise.
Money is a friendly way to picture decimals.
lessons.rule: Money uses two decimal places for paise.
lessons.tip: Think of coins to picture decimal parts.

lessons.title: Reading Decimals
lessons.intro: We read the whole part normally, say 'point', then read each decimal digit one by one.
explanation: 4.25 is read 'four point two five'.
We do NOT say 'twenty-five' after the point — each digit separately.
0.08 is 'zero point zero eight'.
lessons.rule: After the point, read each digit on its own.
lessons.tip: Never group the digits after the point.

lessons.title: Decimals on a Number Line
lessons.intro: Decimals fit neatly between whole numbers on a number line, splitting each gap into ten steps.
explanation: Between 0 and 1 we can mark 0.1, 0.2, ... up to 0.9.
0.5 sits exactly halfway between 0 and 1.
Number lines make decimal sizes easy to see.
lessons.rule: Each unit on the line splits into ten decimal steps.
lessons.tip: 0.5 is always the middle of a unit.

quiz.question: Write 5 tenths as a decimal.
quiz.hint: Tenths go in the first place after the point.

quiz.question: Write 3 and 2 tenths as a decimal.

A pencil is 4 and 5 tenths centimetres long. Write its length as a decimal.
quiz.story: Measuring with a ruler in class.

quiz.question: Riya has 3 rupees and 50 paise. Write this amount as a decimal number of rupees.
quiz.hint: 50 paise is 5 tenths of a rupee.

quiz.question: Write the mixed number 2 and 3/10 as a decimal.
What decimal is exactly halfway between 0 and 1?

lessons.title: Decimal Place Values
lessons.intro: Just like whole numbers, each place after the decimal point has its own value: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
explanation: First place = tenths (1/10), second = hundredths (1/100).
In 0.47 the 4 is 4 tenths and the 7 is 7 hundredths.
Each place is ten times smaller than the one before.
lessons.rule: Decimal places shrink by ten each step right.
lessons.tip: Tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.

steps.text: Name the decimal places from the point.
Each place is ten times smaller.

lessons.title: Hundredths
lessons.intro: The second place after the point is hundredths — a whole split into 100 tiny equal parts.
explanation: 0.01 is one hundredth, 1/100.
0.25 means 25 hundredths, the same as a quarter.
Paise are hundredths of a rupee.
lessons.rule: The second decimal place is hundredths (1/100).
lessons.tip: 0.25 is the same as 1/4.

lessons.title: Place Value of a Digit
lessons.intro: You can name the exact value of any digit in a decimal by its place.
explanation: In 6.38 the 3 is in the tenths place, worth 0.3.
In 6.38 the 8 is in the hundredths place, worth 0.08.
Position matters just as much as in whole numbers.
lessons.rule: A decimal digit's value = digit x its place.
lessons.tip: Point to the digit, then name its place.

lessons.title: Equivalent Decimals
lessons.intro: Adding a zero at the END of a decimal does not change its value — 0.5 and 0.50 are equal.
explanation: 0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500; the extra zeros add nothing.
But 0.05 is NOT the same as 0.5 — position changed!
Trailing zeros are harmless; middle zeros are not.
lessons.rule: Trailing zeros after a decimal don't change its value.
lessons.tip: Only zeros at the very end are 'free'.

lessons.title: Decimals to Fractions
lessons.intro: Every decimal can be written as a fraction over 10, 100, or 1000, then simplified.
explanation: Count the decimal places to choose 10, 100 or 1000.
lessons.rule: Decimal places decide the denominator (10, 100, 1000).
lessons.tip: One place over 10, two places over 100.

quiz.question: In 6.38, what is the place value of the 3? Write it as a decimal.
In 6.38, what is the place value of the 8? Write it as a decimal.
Write 0.25 as a fraction in lowest terms.
Write 0.5 as a fraction in lowest terms.

quiz.hint: Trailing zeros do not change the value.
quiz.story: A classmate asks a tricky question.

quiz.question: Write 0.125 as a fraction in lowest terms.
In 4.062, what is the place value of the 6? Write it as a decimal.

lessons.title: Comparing Decimals
lessons.intro: To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare place by place, just like whole numbers.
explanation: Compare the whole parts first; if equal, move to tenths.
0.7 is greater than 0.65 because 7 tenths beats 6 tenths.
Give each number the same number of decimal places to compare easily.
lessons.rule: Line up the points; compare from the left.
lessons.tip: Add trailing zeros so both have equal places.

steps.text: Make the place counts equal with trailing zeros.

lessons.title: The Trailing-Zero Trick
lessons.intro: Giving decimals the same number of places makes comparing foolproof.
explanation: To compare 0.5 and 0.45, write 0.50 and 0.45.
Now it is clearly 50 vs 45 hundredths, so 0.5 is bigger.
This trick removes all confusion.
lessons.rule: Equalise decimal places before comparing.
lessons.tip: More digits does NOT mean a bigger number.

lessons.title: Ordering Decimals
lessons.intro: Put several decimals in order by comparing them two at a time.
explanation: Descending: 0.4, 0.33, 0.3.
Line up points and sort from the first differing place.
lessons.rule: Sort decimals by their first differing place.
lessons.tip: Equalise places first, then order.

lessons.title: Decimals Between Decimals
lessons.intro: Between any two decimals there is always another decimal — numbers never run out!
explanation: Between 0.3 and 0.4 you can find 0.35.
Between 0.5 and 0.6 you can find 0.55.
Just add another decimal place to fit one in.
lessons.rule: You can always find a decimal between two others.
lessons.tip: Add a place and pick a middle digit.

lessons.title: Comparing in Real Life
lessons.intro: We compare decimals when we weigh things, time races, or measure lengths.
explanation: A 0.75 kg bag is heavier than a 0.7 kg bag.
A runner at 10.8 seconds beats one at 10.85 seconds.
Smaller time wins a race; larger weight is heavier.
lessons.rule: Context tells you whether bigger or smaller is 'better'.
lessons.tip: Read the units to know what you are comparing.

quiz.question: Which is greater: 0.7 or 0.65? Write the greater one.

quiz.hint: Halfway means add a hundredths digit of 5.

lessons.title: Adding Decimals
lessons.intro: Adding decimals is just like adding whole numbers — the one golden rule is to line up the decimal points.
explanation: Stack the numbers so the points are in a column.
Fill empty places with zeros to keep columns neat.
lessons.rule: Line up the decimal points, then add column by column.
lessons.tip: Keep the point in the same column in your answer.

steps.text: Line up the points before adding.

lessons.title: Carrying with Decimals
lessons.intro: When a column adds to 10 or more, carry to the next column — exactly like whole-number addition.
explanation: 0.7 + 0.5 = 1.2 (the tenths made a whole).
The carried 1 moves into the ones place.
The decimal point stays put.
lessons.rule: Carry across the point just like any other column.
lessons.tip: Ten tenths become one whole.

lessons.title: Subtracting Decimals
lessons.intro: Subtraction also needs lined-up points; borrow across columns when needed.
explanation: 1.0 - 0.3 = 0.7 (borrow from the ones place).
Equalise places with zeros before you subtract.
lessons.rule: Line up points; borrow across the point if needed.
lessons.tip: Write 1.0 as 1.0 so columns match.

lessons.title: Money Calculations
lessons.intro: Adding and subtracting money is decimal maths with two places for paise.
explanation: Always keep two decimal places for money.
lessons.rule: Treat money as decimals with two places.
lessons.tip: Line up the rupee points before calculating.

lessons.title: Adding Three Decimals
lessons.intro: You can add several decimals at once — stack them all with points aligned.
explanation: Add the tenths column, then carry if it reaches ten.
More numbers, same rule: line up the points.
lessons.rule: Stack all the numbers by their decimal points.
lessons.tip: Add one column at a time from the right.

quiz.hint: Ten tenths carry to one whole.

quiz.hint: Write 1.80 so places match, then add.

lessons.title: Multiplying by 10, 100, 1000
lessons.intro: Multiplying a decimal by 10 shifts the decimal point one place to the RIGHT — the number grows!
explanation: 0.5 x 10 = 5 (point moves one right).
0.5 x 100 = 50 (point moves two right).
Count the zeros to count the shifts.
lessons.rule: x10 moves the point one place right per zero.
lessons.tip: More zeros, more shifts to the right.

steps.text: Multiplying by 10 shifts the point right.
Each extra zero is one more shift.

lessons.title: Dividing by 10, 100, 1000
lessons.intro: Dividing a decimal by 10 shifts the point one place to the LEFT — the number shrinks.
explanation: 5 / 10 = 0.5 (point moves one left).
5 / 100 = 0.05 (point moves two left).
Add zeros as place-holders if you run out of digits.
lessons.rule: /10 moves the point one place left per zero.
lessons.tip: Fill empty places with zeros.

lessons.title: Multiplying a Decimal by a Whole Number
lessons.intro: Multiply as usual, then place the decimal point so the answer has the right number of decimal places.
explanation: 0.3 x 4 = 1.2 (one decimal place in, one out).
Count decimal places in the question to place the point.
Ignore the point while multiplying, then put it back.
lessons.rule: The answer has as many decimal places as the decimal factor.
lessons.tip: Multiply first, then count places for the point.

lessons.title: Dividing a Decimal by a Whole Number
lessons.intro: Divide as usual and line the decimal point of the answer up with the one inside.
explanation: Keep the point in the quotient above the point inside.
lessons.rule: Place the quotient's point above the dividend's point.
lessons.tip: Divide the digits as normal, keep the point aligned.

lessons.title: Decimal Master Mix
lessons.intro: Now combine everything — multiply, divide and shift points with confidence.
explanation: 0.25 x 4 = 1 (four quarters make a whole).
Always check: does the size of the answer make sense?
lessons.rule: Use point-shifting and place-counting together.
lessons.tip: Estimate first to check your answer is sensible.

quiz.hint: Shift the point one place left.
